title: GMAT Focus Verbal Practice Test 10
instructions: Original exam-style practice test with answers and explanations.

questions.prompt: A market research firm found that consumers who saw a product advertisement spent, on average, 40% more on that brand in the following month than consumers who had not seen the ad. The advertising agency used this data to argue their campaign was effective.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most weakens the advertising agency's argument?
options: A. Consumers who sought out the advertisement were already brand loyalists considering a major purchase
B. The advertising campaign cost $5M over three months
C. The ad was shown only on premium streaming services
D. The brand launched a new product line during the same period
E. Competitors also increased advertising spending during the same period
questions.explanation: If people who saw the ad were already planning to buy (self-selection bias), the higher spending reflects pre-existing intent rather than the ad's persuasive effect.

questions.prompt: A transport analyst argued: 'If we build more roads, traffic will decrease.' Another analyst countered: 'Historically, cities that built more roads saw traffic increase within five years.'
questions.question: The second analyst's response best serves which of the following functions in the debate?
options: A. It provides an alternative interpretation of the first analyst's claim
B. It presents empirical evidence that undermines the first analyst's prediction
C. It demonstrates that road construction is always harmful
D. It suggests the first analyst has incorrect data
E. It proves that traffic will always increase regardless of policy
questions.explanation: The second analyst offers historical evidence ('induced demand') suggesting that more roads actually attract more drivers, contradicting the first analyst's prediction.

questions.prompt: All members of the professional association who completed the certification programme received a salary increase within 12 months. Marcus completed the certification programme. Therefore, Marcus will receive a salary increase within 12 months.
questions.question: Which of the following most closely parallels the logical structure of the argument above?
options: A. Most people who exercise regularly live longer. Jana exercises. Therefore, Jana will live longer than average.
B. Some companies that invest in R&D are profitable. TechCo invests in R&D. Therefore, TechCo is profitable.
C. Every student who passes the bar exam becomes a lawyer. Sarah passed the bar exam. Therefore, Sarah is a lawyer.
D. Employees who exceed targets generally get promoted. Daniel exceeded his target. Daniel got promoted.
E. All birds have wings. Penguins are birds. Therefore, penguins can fly.
questions.explanation: The original argument follows the valid syllogism: All A→B, Marcus is A, therefore Marcus→B. Option A mirrors this exactly with 'all' not 'most/some'.

questions.prompt: A survey found that 70% of workers who reported high job satisfaction also reported sleeping 7–9 hours per night. The survey authors concluded that sleeping 7–9 hours causes job satisfaction.
questions.question: Which of the following conclusions is most strongly supported by the survey data?
options: A. Improving sleep quality will increase job satisfaction for most workers
B. Dissatisfied workers always sleep fewer than 7 hours
C. Employers should implement nap rooms to improve satisfaction
D. Job satisfaction and adequate sleep are associated in the survey population
E. Workers who sleep 8 hours are more productive than those who sleep 6
questions.explanation: The data shows an association (correlation), not causation. The only safely supported conclusion is that the two variables are associated in this survey population.

questions.prompt: City X has 12% more police officers per capita than City Y. City X also has a 12% lower crime rate than City Y. A politician argued that hiring more police reduces crime.
questions.question: To evaluate the politician's argument, it would be most useful to determine:
options: A. Whether the police officers in City X are better trained
B. Whether crime in both cities is measured using the same methodology
C. Whether the cities differ in poverty rates, population density, or other factors correlated with crime
D. Whether the crime reduction happened before or after police hiring increased
E. All of the above
questions.explanation: All four questions help evaluate whether the police-to-crime correlation reflects a causal relationship or whether confounding variables, measurement differences, or reversed causality explain the data.

questions.prompt: An environmental group claimed: 'Protecting wetlands prevents flooding, therefore we should protect all wetlands.' A developer responded: 'Some wetlands are not near flood-prone areas, so protecting them does not prevent flooding.'
questions.question: The developer's response most effectively challenges which aspect of the environmental group's argument?
options: A. The claim that wetlands prevent flooding
B. The conclusion that all wetlands should be protected
C. The implication that flooding is always preventable
D. The premise that wetlands are worth preserving
E. The assumption that all wetlands have equal flood-prevention value
questions.explanation: The developer doesn't deny that wetlands prevent flooding generally, but challenges the blanket application by showing the flood-prevention benefit varies by location.

questions.prompt: A fashion retailer noticed that stores playing upbeat music had 20% higher sales per hour than stores playing slow music. The marketing team concluded they should switch all stores to upbeat music immediately.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most strengthen the marketing team's recommendation?
options: A. A controlled experiment with randomly assigned music found the same 20% difference
B. Customers reported preferring a relaxed shopping atmosphere
C. The upbeat music stores were in higher-traffic mall locations
D. Sales staff performed better when the music was upbeat
E. Upbeat music has been shown to increase heart rate and impulse purchases in laboratory studies
questions.explanation: A controlled, randomised experiment eliminates confounding factors (location, store size) and directly supports the causal claim that upbeat music drives higher sales.

questions.prompt: A newspaper editorial argued: 'Crime statistics show that areas with higher unemployment have higher crime rates. Therefore, reducing unemployment is the most effective way to fight crime.'
questions.question: Which of the following most weakens the editorial's conclusion?
options: A. Employment programmes have reduced crime in some pilot cities
B. Crime rates are influenced by many factors beyond unemployment
C. The editorial does not define 'crime' precisely
D. Reducing unemployment is expensive and politically difficult
E. Some high-unemployment areas have low crime rates due to strong community cohesion
questions.explanation: Even if unemployment correlates with crime, many other variables (education, policing, social programmes) also affect crime rates, making unemployment reduction potentially not the 'most effective' single strategy.

questions.prompt: A university president argued that because students with higher SAT scores perform better academically, the admissions office should give more weight to SAT scores to improve overall student performance.
questions.question: The president's argument is flawed because it:
options: A. Ignores that SAT preparation courses can inflate scores
B. Assumes that selecting for high SAT scorers will raise overall performance rather than simply filtering applicants
C. Does not consider the diversity implications of the policy
D. Fails to define 'academic performance' precisely
E. Both A and B
questions.explanation: Even if SAT scores correlate with performance among admitted students, selecting for high scorers changes the pool — it doesn't guarantee that the selected group will perform better than a more holistically-selected group.

questions.prompt: A financial adviser told a client: 'The stock market has risen every year for the past five years, so it is safe to invest heavily in equities now.' The client then invested 90% of her savings in equities.
questions.question: The adviser's reasoning is most analogous to which of the following?
options: A. Investing in diversified funds reduces portfolio risk over time
B. A stock's five-year return is a better predictor of future performance than its one-year return
C. Because a coin has landed heads five times in a row, it is more likely to land tails next time
D. Historical market data is unreliable because markets change structurally over time
E. Companies with consistent earnings growth tend to have stable stock prices
questions.explanation: Both commit the gambler's fallacy — assuming that a streak of past outcomes changes the probability of future outcomes for an independent event.

questions.prompt: A retail chain found that stores with loyalty programmes had 35% higher annual sales than stores without them. The chain concluded that loyalty programmes directly cause increased sales.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the conclusion?
options: A. Loyalty programmes cost approximately 8% of the revenue they generate
B. Customers report feeling more valued when using a loyalty programme
C. Competitors without loyalty programmes have seen declining sales
D. Stores in wealthier districts both have higher sales and are more likely to pilot loyalty programmes
E. The loyalty programme was introduced simultaneously with a store renovation
questions.explanation: If wealthier districts drive both higher sales and loyalty programme adoption, the correlation doesn't imply causation — a confounding variable explains both.

questions.prompt: A tech startup spent $2M on social media advertising and saw user sign-ups rise by 60,000 over three months. The CFO argued this proved social media advertising is cost-effective for customer acquisition.
questions.question: Which of the following would most strengthen the CFO's conclusion?
options: A. Other advertising channels were suspended during the same three months
B. Sign-ups had already been rising at 20,000 per month before the campaign
C. Social media platforms reported the campaign reached 5 million unique users
D. Competitors saw no change in sign-ups over the same period
E. The lifetime value of a new user averages $50
questions.explanation: If each user is worth $50 lifetime and 60,000 signed up, revenue = $3M on $2M spend — making the acquisition cost-effective.

questions.prompt: A study found that neighbourhoods with higher tree canopy coverage have lower summer temperatures than neighbourhoods with less tree cover. City planners proposed planting more trees to reduce urban heat.
questions.question: Which of the following most accurately describes the flaw in the proposal's reasoning?
options: A. It treats a correlation as evidence of a causal relationship
B. It assumes that lower temperatures are always desirable
C. It ignores that tree planting is expensive
D. It fails to consider that trees require water
E. It overlooks that some neighbourhoods may not have space for trees
questions.explanation: The study shows correlation between trees and lower temperatures, but neighbourhoods with trees may differ in other ways (e.g., less pavement, more parks) that also reduce heat.

questions.prompt: An airline introduced a new boarding policy — allowing all passengers to board simultaneously regardless of seat row — and found average boarding time fell from 28 minutes to 19 minutes. The operations team concluded the new policy was responsible.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken this conclusion?
options: A. Passengers reported higher satisfaction with the new policy
B. The airline also reduced the number of carry-on bags allowed during the same period
C. Competing airlines have not adopted similar policies
D. Boarding time varies naturally between 15 and 35 minutes
E. The new policy was introduced on routes with larger aircraft
questions.explanation: If carry-on restrictions (not the boarding order) reduced the time taken to stow luggage, the boarding policy itself may not have caused the improvement.

questions.prompt: A consulting firm found that companies that hired its services increased revenue by an average of 18% within one year. The firm uses this as evidence that its services drive revenue growth.
questions.question: The argument above is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it:
options: A. Does not define what type of consulting services were provided
B. Ignores that some companies declined in revenue after hiring the firm
C. Fails to compare the companies' growth with industry-wide growth trends
D. Does not specify what time period is covered by the data
E. Compares incomparable companies across different industries
questions.explanation: Without comparing to the baseline industry growth rate, the 18% may simply reflect normal market conditions rather than the firm's impact.

questions.prompt: A government health agency reported that regions where the population consumes olive oil as their primary cooking fat have significantly lower rates of cardiovascular disease than regions that use butter. The agency concluded that replacing butter with olive oil in the diet would reduce heart disease.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most undermine the agency's conclusion?
options: A. Olive oil contains monounsaturated fats linked to heart health
B. Heart disease rates have been declining globally regardless of fat consumption
C. The study followed individuals for 10 years
D. Regions using olive oil also have Mediterranean diets rich in vegetables and fish
E. Olive oil is more expensive than butter in most markets
questions.explanation: If olive oil regions also differ in diet (more fish, vegetables) and lifestyle, the lower heart disease rate cannot be attributed to olive oil alone.

questions.prompt: Hospital records show that patients who received follow-up phone calls from their doctors within 48 hours of discharge had a 40% lower readmission rate than those who did not receive calls. A hospital administrator recommended implementing mandatory follow-up calls for all patients.
questions.question: Which of the following identifies a potential flaw in the administrator's reasoning?
options: A. The cost of implementing mandatory calls would be prohibitive
B. Some patients do not have phones
C. Patients prefer in-person follow-up visits to phone calls
D. Phone calls are less effective than written instructions
E. Doctors who proactively call patients may also be more thorough in their overall care
questions.explanation: Doctors who voluntarily call patients may also provide better care in hospital, meaning it's doctor quality — not the call itself — that reduces readmissions.

questions.prompt: A pharmaceutical company found that patients who took Drug X for six months experienced a 30% reduction in chronic pain symptoms. The company concluded Drug X is effective for treating chronic pain.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most weakens the conclusion?
options: A. A control group taking a placebo experienced a 28% reduction in symptoms
B. Drug X has minor side effects including nausea
C. The study included only 50 participants
D. Chronic pain affects millions of people worldwide
E. Drug X is expensive compared to existing treatments
questions.explanation: If the placebo group had a nearly identical 28% improvement, the drug's effect is indistinguishable from the placebo effect.

questions.prompt: A university fitness centre reported that students who exercised at least three times per week had a GPA 0.4 points higher on average than students who exercised less. The director concluded that encouraging exercise would improve academic performance.
questions.question: Which of the following most strengthens the director's conclusion?
options: A. Students with higher GPAs may have more structured schedules that allow for regular exercise
B. Exercise has been shown to improve blood flow to the brain in laboratory studies
C. The university's highest-achieving students attend the fitness centre most frequently
D. Exercise programmes are popular at peer universities
E. Students who exercise report feeling less stressed
questions.explanation: A biological mechanism linking exercise to brain function provides direct support for the causal claim that exercise improves academic performance.

questions.prompt: A city's traffic authority found that intersections with red-light cameras had 22% fewer accidents than those without. The authority recommended installing cameras at all major intersections.
questions.question: Which of the following is the most serious concern about the authority's recommendation?
options: A. Cameras might violate driver privacy
B. The cost of cameras is high
C. Intersections chosen for cameras may have already been due for safety upgrades
D. Some drivers find cameras distracting
E. Cameras only capture rear-end collisions
questions.explanation: If cameras were installed at intersections already scheduled for safety improvements (repaving, better lighting), those improvements — not the cameras — may account for the accident reduction.

questions.passageText: The concept of neuroplasticity — the brain's ability to reorganise itself by forming new neural connections throughout life — has fundamentally altered how neuroscientists and educators think about learning. For much of the twentieth century, the dominant view held that the adult brain was largely fixed, with neural pathways established by early childhood remaining permanent. This view is now known to be incomplete. Research beginning in the 1960s and accelerating in the late 1990s demonstrated that the adult brain retains a surprising capacity for structural change in response to experience, injury, and learning. Studies of patients recovering from strokes showed that functions lost due to brain damage could sometimes be partially recovered as neighbouring regions of the brain assumed control of disrupted processes. Parallel research in healthy adults confirmed that intensive practice of a skill, from learning a musical instrument to mastering a new language, produces measurable changes in brain structure, particularly in the cortical regions associated with the practised skill.
questions.prompt: According to the passage, what was the dominant view of the adult brain for much of the 20th century?
options: A. The brain continuously forms new neural connections throughout adulthood
B. Neuroplasticity is highest in adults recovering from injury
C. Brain structure is largely fixed after early childhood
D. Learning a new skill has no measurable effect on brain structure
questions.explanation: Based on the passage content about Neuroplasticity.

readingPassages.title: Business and Society
readingPassages.text: Researchers studying organisational behaviour have found that teams with diverse cognitive styles outperform homogeneous teams on complex problem-solving tasks. However, this benefit is not automatic — diverse teams require skilled facilitation to avoid miscommunication and conflict. When managed effectively, the creative tension between different thinking styles produces more innovative solutions than teams where all members approach problems similarly.
